newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: US says WTO has historic chance on infotech deal.
newsitem.headline: US says WTO has historic chance on infotech deal.

text.p: The United States urged World Trade Organisation (WTO) minsters on Monday to pave the way for a more connected global economy by agreeing to eliminate tariffs on a host of information technologies.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who has been pushing to make a global Information Technology Agreement (ITA) the crowning achievement of the first WTO ministerial meeting, said it would help businesses become more competitive in the global economy by putting lower cost technologies and information in their hands.

"That's why we must reach an agreement this week," she said in a speech to the opening session of the WTO meeting. "Remaining issues are ripe for decision. We have an historic opportunity to eliminate tariffs on these products. We must seize it."

U.S. officials have been holding intense discussions with the European Union, Japan and other trading partners attending the WTO meeting this week in Singapore, in an effort to strike a deal by the closing session on Friday, December 13.

"The Information Technology Agreement, would be the first concrete demonstration of the WTO's ability to move forward in concert with the changing world around us," Barshefsky said. "By creating a tariff-free environment for trade in information technology products, we can help lower consumer costs, make our businesses more competitive and give our entire economies the benefits that flow from access to greater information."
U.S. officials and business representatives attending the Singapore conference have said they are hopeful remaining differences, particularly with the European Union, can be settled.
A successful ITA agreement at the WTO meeting would be an important feather in Barshefsky's cap at a time she is hoping to remove "acting" from her current title.

President Clinton is expected to nominate her as U.S. Trade Representative. But her appointment would be subject to approval by the Senate, where she would likely face tough questioning by lawmakers increasingly wary of the impact of global free trade on U.S. workers.

Barshefsky also faces a tough fight with lawmakers next year over legislation that would give her authority to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement -- comprised of Mexico, the United States and Canada -- to include Chile. She would like to be able to show that free trade agreements can open markets to important U.S. business sectors.

U.S. officials also believe the ITA could have a domino effect on other pending trade deals -- global agreements to open telecommunications markets and financial services markets to more foreign competitors.

A successful ITA would provide an important momentum to complete those negotiations, which so far have failed to yield agreement. Likewise, U.S. officials say privately, failure of the ITA this week would mostly likely doom those other trade pacts.

Negotiators face a February 15 deadline for a deal on basic telecommunications services and Barshefsky urged other countries to follow the lead of Europe and the United States, which have recently improved their offers.
But she warned that there would be no deal if offers from other countries proved to be insufficient.

"Today the United States accounts for nearly 50 percent of all telecom revenue worldwide," she said in her speech. "We cannot and will not, settle for a situation where we are unable to operate in the other half of the world's markets. We are ready to lead by making the first best offer, but we cannot succeed unless others come forward on a mutual basis."

Trade negotiators also hope to win agreement by the end of next year on lowering trade barriers on financial services. The first effort at a deal failed, but Barshefsky said agreement could be reached if key countries improve their commitments to lower barriers.
